newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuelan bolivar to stay stable in bands - Casas.
newsitem.headline: Venezuelan bolivar to stay stable in bands - Casas.

text.p: The Venezuelan bolivar is not following a hidden "crawling peg system," nor is it a fully-fledged exchange rate anchor, Central Bank Governor Antonio Casas Gonzalez said.

"The Central Bank's message is that we're going to continue with a stable exchange rate; stable within the bands, because I've never said that we were going to anchor the bolivar," Casas told reporters after a conference.
Venezuela continues to pursue an inflation-fighting strong-bolivar policy.

Although the currency ostensibly floats between slowly depreciating bands set by Central Bank intervention, the exchange rate has little changed since price and currency controls were removed in April 1996, despite 70 percent-plus inflation.

That stability has become a totem for the foreign exchange market, even as critics say the policy, which has effectively used the currency as a exchange rate anchor to bear down on inflation, has increasingly left the bolivar over-valued.
Last week, however, the bolivar uncharacteristically slipped 0.3 percent, fueled by -- and in turn fueling -- expectations of faster depreciation.
"It's true the market has heated up recently, due to expectations fed by the press," Casas said.

But he said the bolivar's recent movements merely showed "the flexibility of the exchange rate within the exchange bands system," adding that Monday's session had seen the bolivar firm slightly to its 482.75/483.75 per dollar close.
The Central Bank has never said "the exchange rate will be totally anchored," said Casas.
By midday Tuesday the bolivar had softened to 483.05/482.90 per dollar.
